The instruction is simple: write whatever comes to you. But the blank page has a way of making the simple feel impossible. It sits there, white and patient, and the cursor blinks like a metronome, measuring silence. I think about the word "whatever"—how it can be a shrug, an invitation, a warning. Whatever comes. As if thoughts were weather, arriving without permission, leaving without goodbye. I could write about that, but I'm already writing about writing, which is the first thing the mind does when asked to produce something from nothing. It folds in on itself, becomes a hall of mirrors. Every sentence is a door, and behind every door is another door, and somewhere in the distance there's a room where the real words are hiding, but I'm not sure I have the key.

I have a thousand words. That's not a lot, actually. A thousand words is maybe a long essay, a short story's opening, a letter you never send. My high school senior thesis was seven thousand words, and I wrote it in a weekend, fueled by energy drinks and the fear of God. Now a thousand feels like a mountain. The older I get, the more I understand that quantity doesn't equal truth. You can say a thousand true things and still be lying, or you can say one true thing and feel it in your teeth. I want to write something true, but I don't know what that is yet. The truth isn't a destination. It's more like a smell you catch when you're not looking for it—rain on hot pavement, a bakery at dawn, the particular mustiness of a basement that hasn't been opened in years.

When I was nine, I spent a summer at my grandmother's house. It had a screened porch that looked out over a yard that was fifty percent dandelions. I used to sit on the steps and pull the white heads apart, scattering seeds into a wind I couldn't see. I remember thinking that each seed might land somewhere and become a new flower, and that all those flowers might one day cover the world, and that this was both beautiful and terrifying. That's how I feel about words now. You put them out, and you don't know where they land. They drift over fences, into other people's lives, through the quiet rooms of strangers who will never meet you. Some take root. Some don't. Some become weeds. Some become wishes. The "whatever" in the prompt is the wind. I can't control it. I can only open my hand.

But maybe that's the point. The instruction isn't asking for a masterpiece. It's asking for an exercise in letting go. For ten minutes, I am allowed to think without a reason, to write without a blueprint, to be the kind of person who believes in first drafts. That should be a relief, but I've been trained to see purpose in everything. I want every sentence to earn its keep. I want the ending to justify the beginning. I want the reader—whoever you are—to feel that this was worth your time. And in wanting that, I strangle the very thing I'm trying to release. So I have to remind myself: a thousand words is not a test. It's a walk. You don't walk to arrive. You walk because the sun is out, because the street is interesting, because your body needs to move.

I think about the last time I took a walk without a destination. It was autumn, and the air smelled like woodsmoke and regret. I passed a house with a carved pumpkin rotting on the porch. Its face was collapsing, a jack-o'-lantern becoming a skull. I felt sorry for it, then realized I was feeling sorry for a piece of fruit. That's the thing about being human: we attach meaning to everything. The mind is a pattern-making machine. It takes the chaos of the world and stitches it into stories—some true, some useful, most of them just a way of passing the time.

I want to say something about the people I love, but they're not here. They're scattered across time zones and busy schedules, existing in photos and voice notes and the specific way they say my name. I love them more than I can put into words, which is strange because I'm supposed to be putting words into the world. But "I love you" never feels like enough, and "more than anything" is just a quantity without a shape. So I write around it instead. I describe the way my sister laughs when she's tired, the way my father hums while he cooks, the way a friend once drove an hour to sit with me in silence because I couldn't stop crying. Those are the words that matter. They don't say "I love you." They say "I was there." And maybe that's all love is: showing up for somebody's chaos, not to fix it but to sit beside it.

The screen is filling up. I can see the end approaching, a shoreline growing clearer. I haven't written about the war in the east, or the fires in the west, or the other catastrophes that live in the headlines and then vanish into the next one. I haven't written anything useful. I've written about a pumpkin, a grandmother's dandelions, and the impossible task of asking a blank page to become a room. But perhaps that is what "whatever comes" really means. It means trusting that what arrives is enough. It means letting the mind wander until it finds what it was looking for, even if it never says it out loud. I don't know if I've found anything. But I've filled a thousand words, and the cursor is no longer blinking. It's just waiting, like I'll be waiting, for the next time someone says, "Write whatever comes to you." And I will. And it will come. It always does.
